synopsis: RAND's Driving to Safety report by Kalra and Paddock, published in April 2016, argues that road-driving demonstrations of autonomous-vehicle reliability require hundreds of millions, sometimes hundreds of billions, of miles—taking existing fleets tens or hundreds of years [f6920, f6921, f5466]. Its benchmarks include 275 million failure-free miles to demonstrate, at 95% confidence, a fatality rate no worse than 1.09 per 100 million miles, and about 11 billion miles to demonstrate a 20% improvement with 95% confidence and 80% power [f6922, f6923]. A separate 2019 conservative Bayesian analysis illustrates sensitivity to prior assumptions: a strong prior with 90% prior confidence reduces the 275-million-mile requirement to 69 million, while a weak prior increases it to 476 million [f6901, f6902]. The booklet transfers RAND's statistical logic, but not its road-mile numbers, to off-road per-encounter detection and intervention claims, recommending simulation, statistics and targeted tests rather than reliance on field hours [f6664, f15826]. RAND also developed assumption-based planning, documented in 1993 and 2002, which the booklet adopts to track load-bearing assumptions, failure signposts and hedges [f9557, f15818, f16345]. Despite repeated use of RAND as an established statistical foundation, the skeptic's review says RAND 2016 was a relevant lead that was not verified in the research, leaving a source-verification tension [f7400, f11203].
